item.text: {"text":"[Betello et al., ECIR 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.13165) study training-data deletions followed by retraining, using SASRec and GRU4Rec. Removing recent interactions caused substantial accuracy losses, reaching 60% NDCG; beginning/middle deletions had little effect in their experiments. Ranking instability also occurred with similar aggregate accuracy, so overlap alone does not establish recommendation quality. These results motivate position-aware probes but do not establish that frozen-model inference sensitivity predicts gains from retraining, particularly for HSTU. Random deletion controls matched by deletion count and eligible users, plus shuffling that preserves the last item, are reasonable diagnostic extensions—not validated protocols from this paper. Treat their ability to guide changes as a hypothesis; assess association with actual validation HR@10 improvements across authorized trials.\n\nDefine top-k overlap explicitly as |A∩B|/k for two k-item lists; Jaccard instead divides by |A∪B|. Both ignore order. The authors’ [FRBO implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/federicosiciliano/finite_rank_biased_rbo/main/frbo.py) computes, for equal-length k-item rankings, FRBO@k = [(1−p)/(1−p^k)] Σ(d=1…k) p^(d−1)|A₁:d∩B₁:d|/d, then averages across users; higher values mean greater stability. Report k and p, ensure unique items, and use identical candidate sets and exclusion rules. Identical lists score 1; disjoint lists score 0. Distinguish this normalized finite sum from [Webber et al.’s extrapolated RBO](https://www.codalism.com/research/papers/wmz10_tois.pdf), which estimates agreement beyond the observed prefix. Report inference perturbations as input sensitivity, separately from robustness measured after retraining."}
